story.logline: You buy a few sugary drinks a week. Then a tax arrives. You might expect the higher price to cut your sugar. But changed recipes cut more. So what does the tax change for you?

question: What would change for me if there was a tax on sugary drinks?

source.title: What a sugar tax on soft drinks changes
quotes: A typical design adds 20% to the shelf price of drinks with a lot of added sugar.
Shops pass most of the tax on to customers: studies find prices rise by about 80% of the tax.
For every 10% rise in price, people buy about 12% less of the taxed drinks, according to a large review of studies.
In one country, the sugar in soft drinks sold fell by about 30% within three years, mostly because recipes changed, not because people bought fewer drinks.
Faced with the tax, many reformulate their drinks to fall below the sugar threshold.
In practice, the biggest effect often comes from companies changing recipes before the tax even starts.
It takes a larger share of income from poorer households, who drink more soft drinks.
The money raised goes to the government.

ask.question: About how many sugary soft drinks do you buy a week?
ask.help: Count regular cans and bottles, not diet ones. Zero is fine.

ask.question: What does one of those drinks usually cost?
ask.help: Check a recent receipt or the shelf price.

explain.caption: A tax lands on sugary drinks. What changes for you?
You buy a few sugary drinks each week.
The tax only hits drinks with sugar above a set line.
Shops pass most of the tax on at the till.
Pricier drinks, so you buy fewer and drink less sugar.
The drinks you still buy cost more. That goes to government.
Drink makers change recipes to slip under the line.
But new recipes cut more of your sugar than buying less.
Your sugar falls, mostly without you changing a thing.
Now make it yours. Your drinks, your numbers.

simulate.prompt: Try a bigger or smaller tax. Then try your own drinks.

tradeoffs: New recipes cut the most sugar, but drinks just under the line still contain sugar.
The money from the tax can pay for school sport or healthy meals. But most of it comes from people who drink the most.
It takes a larger share of income from poorer households, who drink more soft drinks.
A bigger tax cuts more sugar, but costs regular buyers more at the till.
leftOut: The article gives no figure for how many makers change recipes. This page sets that share so that the model gives the article's 30% fall. It makes the share grow in step with the tax.
How much sugar a changed recipe loses is an assumption. It depends on where the tax puts the line.
People can switch to untaxed sugary foods, which this model does not count.
The buying response comes from a review of many studies. One country or one person can differ. Very large taxes are outside what the studies covered.
The 30% fall took three years in one country. This model shows the end result, not how long it takes.
The model leaves out health effects, such as weight or tooth decay. Tax rules and lines differ by country, so check what applies to you.
questionsToAsk: Where exactly is the sugar line, and which drinks fall under it?
Will the money raised go to anything specific, such as school sport or healthy meals?
What has happened to sugar intake in places that already have this tax?
How will the tax affect households on low incomes?
